q: A study found walking 10 minutes after each meal curbed post-meal blood sugar better than walking 30 minutes at once.
head: True. 10 minutes after meals did better.
why: A randomized crossover trial in adults with type 2 diabetes. The same change won't necessarily happen for everyone.

q: HbA1c on a health checkup is strongly affected by the meal you ate right before the test.
head: False. It mostly reflects the past 1-2 months.
why: HbA1c reflects blood sugar over several months, weighted toward the past one to two months, rather than your last meal.

q: In the DCCT type 1 diabetes trial, the intensive therapy group had about 76% less onset of retinopathy.
head: True. About 76% less.
why: Microalbuminuria was about 39% lower and clinical neuropathy about 60% lower. But this was in people with diabetes; it can't be applied directly to healthy people.

q: Reviews of the research have confirmed that blue-light glasses reduce eye strain from computer work.
head: False. Probably no short-term advantage.
why: A 2023 Cochrane review concluded they probably offer no short-term advantage over ordinary lenses for reducing eye strain.

q: In Japan, groups including the Japanese Ophthalmological Society urge caution about children wearing blue-light glasses.
head: True. They issued a statement in 2021.
why: The reasons: screens give off less blue light than the outdoors on a cloudy day, and children need sunlight to develop.

q: The drop in eye strain from 20-20-20 rule breaks lasted even after people stopped taking the breaks.
head: False. It was gone a week later.
why: Two weeks of software reminders to take breaks reduced eye strain, but a week after people stopped using it, the improvement hadn't lasted.

q: The most consistent finding in blueberry research is that they're "good for the brain."
head: False. The consistent one is vessel function.
why: What's most consistently shown is an effect on blood vessel function. Some cognitive tasks show promising results, but it isn't settled.

q: Blueberries baked into a snack lost about 42% of their anthocyanins, yet vessel response rose about as much.
head: True. About the same, up to 6 hours.
why: A crossover trial in 10 healthy people: FMD up to 6 hours after eating matched the unprocessed drink. It can't tell us if long-term effects are the same.

q: In a 6-month trial of adults with metabolic syndrome eating blueberries, insulin resistance improved.
head: False. It didn't change.
why: In the 6-month RCT, insulin resistance, pulse wave velocity, blood pressure, and nitric oxide did not change.

q: According to the description of Hard to Break, habits are just behaviors you want to quit.
head: False. Some habits hold up daily life.
why: Daily routines and the way we use tools also happen without much thought thanks to habit. Some behaviors you want to change; others you want to keep.

q: The "pleasure" covered in The Compass of Pleasure includes good deeds like giving to charity.
head: True. Even giving to charity.
why: It lines up sex, drugs, alcohol, high-calorie food, gambling, and even giving to charity from one point of view: the "pleasure circuit."

q: The Compass of Pleasure is a book about pushing pleasure and addiction away as "bad things."
head: False. It explains them as mechanisms.
why: Its appeal is understanding pleasure and addiction as mechanisms. Getting absorbed and being unable to stop both extend from the same brain processes.

q: If your only reason for changing jobs is "I hate my company," the same thing is likely to happen at the next one.
head: True. Look for a reason to go toward.
why: The World's Gentlest Guide to Finding "What You Want to Do" helps you find a reason to go toward something, beyond your reason to run from something.

q: The 100-Year Life recommends thinking of life in three stages: education, work, retirement.
head: False. It questions the three stages.
why: Its view of not thinking of life as "education, work, retirement" helps you see a job change as one move within several decades.

q: Research says a habit forms if you keep it up for 21 days.
head: False. It ranged from 18 to 254 days.
why: How long a habit takes to become automatic varies a lot by person and behavior: from 18 to 254 days in research. "21 days" is best not used as a guide.

q: A large replication across 23 labs found almost no support for the idea that willpower gets used up.
head: True. It found almost no effect.
why: The large-scale replication of ego depletion found almost no effect. Read "willpower is limited, so save it" without taking it as settled.

q: An analysis combining 88 studies found grit strongly linked to performance.
head: False. Moderate or weaker.
why: The link between grit and performance was moderate or weaker, and grit overlapped heavily with conscientiousness. It isn't the one force that decides success.

q: Both Nietzsche and Frankl held that people can find meaning in any situation.
head: False. They stand on opposite sides.
why: Nietzsche said meaning isn't given, while Frankl held that people can find meaning in any situation.

q: Fromm argued that while people seek freedom, they sometimes give it up themselves.
head: True. Unable to bear loneliness and anxiety.
why: Escape from Freedom argues people sometimes can't bear the loneliness and anxiety that come with freedom, and give it up. Written in 1941.

q: Camus's "absurd" means the world itself is absurd.
head: False. It's a mismatch between us and the world.
why: People demand meaning, and the world gives no answer. The absurd arises where the two face each other.

q: Camus portrayed Sisyphus, pushing his boulder forever, as "the unhappiest man."
head: False. "One must imagine Sisyphus happy."
why: The book ends with that line. The struggle itself toward the heights is enough to fill a man's heart.

q: Camus called it "revolt" to keep living while knowing there is no meaning.
head: True. He called it "revolt."
why: Not jumping to the hope that there must be a meaning, but knowing there is none and living anyway. That is "revolt."

q: Even between people with the most and fewest "morning" gene variants, sleep timing differed by only about 25 minutes.
head: True. About 25 minutes on average.
why: A study of about 700,000 people found 351 regions linked to being a morning person. Genes create a tendency, but don't decide it alone.

q: People are most night-owlish around age 20, then drift back toward mornings.
head: True. Found in a study of 25,000 people.
why: Children are morning types, become later types as they grow, reach their latest around age 20, then drift back toward mornings.

q: After a week of camping with only natural light, morning types' body clocks shifted earlier the most.
head: False. Night types shifted the most.
why: In the eight-person experiment, those who had been night types shifted the most, narrowing the gap with the morning types.

q: Coffee's tendency to raise cholesterol was barely seen when it was brewed through a paper filter.
head: True. The paper catches the oily compounds.
why: The rise was large with unfiltered coffee, such as boiled coffee. The paper filter is thought to catch the oily compounds.

q: In Japan, "caffeine-less coffee" is coffee with zero caffeine.
head: False. 90% or more removed.
why: In Japan, the industry standard is that it has had 90% or more of its caffeine removed. Drink a lot, and you take in caffeine accordingly.

q: In a Norwegian study of 500,000+ people, risk of death was lowest among drinkers of unfiltered coffee.
head: False. 1-4 cups of filtered coffee a day.
why: Lowest risk was with 1-4 cups of filtered coffee a day. It's observational, so brewing method alone can't be called the cause.

q: In one experiment, 400 mg of caffeine taken 6 hours before bed still cut sleep by more than an hour.
head: True. People barely noticed.
why: A small experiment with 12 healthy people. 400 mg is a large amount, about four cups of coffee. We can't say the same happens with one cup.

q: Pooling the research, people who drank no coffee had the lowest health risks.
head: False. Lowest around 3-4 cups a day.
why: An umbrella review of more than 200 meta-analyses found risk lowest around 3-4 cups a day. But most are observational: association, not effect.

q: The 400 mg daily caffeine guide for healthy adults is about four 150 mL cups of drip coffee.
head: True. About 90 mg a cup, so about four.
why: Drip coffee has about 60 mg per 100 mL, so about 90 mg per 150 mL. During pregnancy or breastfeeding, the guide is 200 mg a day (about two cups).

q: One theory says we compare ourselves with others when there's no clear standard.
head: True. Social comparison theory, 1954.
why: Festinger proposed that without a clear standard, people check where they stand by comparing with others. It may not be a sign of weak will.

q: Reviews of the research say social media lowers well-being regardless of how it's used.
head: False. It depends on how you use it.
why: Passive use, just scrolling, tends to go with lower well-being, while active use, interacting with people, can sometimes raise it.

q: Alkalizing cocoa barely changes how many flavanols it has.
head: False. About 35 mg fell to about 4 mg.
why: Non-alkalized cocoa averaged about 35 mg per gram, while heavily alkalized cocoa had about 4 mg.

q: The "cacao" percentage on chocolate includes cocoa butter, the fat of the cacao bean.
head: True. It's a total that includes the fat.
why: It's the total of cocoa mass, cocoa powder, cocoa butter, and so on. Flavanol content tracked closely with the fat-free cocoa solids.

q: In US testing, organic cacao products had less lead and cadmium.
head: False. Organic didn't have less.
why: A study of 72 cacao products in the US found organic ones didn't have less. Results may not apply directly to products elsewhere.

q: In the large COSMOS trial, cocoa extract significantly reduced total cardiovascular events.
head: False. Primary outcome not significant.
why: Hazard ratio 0.90, not significant. The 27% drop in cardiovascular death was a secondary outcome; the researchers said further research is needed.

q: In US testing, 23 of 28 dark chocolates exceeded a state's daily limit for heavy metals in about 28 g.
head: True. Only five were within limits.
why: A consumer organization's testing report, not a peer-reviewed paper. US products, judged by California's standards.

q: Cocoa products lowered blood pressure more in people with normal blood pressure.
head: False. No significant fall in them.
why: In trials of people with high blood pressure only, systolic fell by about 4 mmHg; almost no effect with normal pressure. Not big enough to replace medication.

q: Jeans worn for 15 months without washing had about as many bacteria as jeans worn after a wash.
head: True. But it was one person, one pair.
why: Even in the crotch, almost the same as after two weeks of wear following a wash, and the bacteria were ordinary skin bacteria. Not a peer-reviewed test.

q: Of all the water a pair of jeans uses in its lifetime, washing after purchase takes the most.
head: False. 68% goes to growing cotton.
why: One pair used 3,781 liters of water: 68% for growing cotton, 23% for washing and care after purchase (the maker's own assessment).

q: No material other than leather combined strength, flex durability, and breathability.
head: True. Compared with nine alternatives.
why: A German institute tested leather, synthetic leather, and alternative leathers such as cactus under the same conditions. Some beat it on single measures, not all.

q: A 2023 review still found no clear conclusion on antiperspirant aluminum and breast cancer.
head: True. The studies were inconsistent.
why: No clear conclusion could be drawn. There's no basis for calling it "dangerous," but the assessments don't entirely agree either.

q: People committed to a purpose can act despite being disliked, but not because they've stopped caring.
head: True. It just drops in priority.
why: The need for connection doesn't vanish with a purpose. Others' opinions haven't disappeared; their ranking for your attention has changed.

q: Older adults who rested 10 minutes after learning a story remembered it better even 7 days later.
head: True. The difference lasted to day 7.
why: In Dewar and colleagues' experiment, 10 minutes of wakeful rest improved memory not only shortly after but also seven days later, without extra study time.

q: Ideas improved most after a break of doing absolutely nothing.
head: False. After about 12 minutes of easy tasks.
why: In Baird and colleagues' experiment, the biggest gain on creativity problems came after about 12 minutes of an undemanding task, with more mind wandering.

q: Research shows that zoning out for 20 minutes is optimal.
head: False. There's no basis for 20 minutes.
why: In the key studies, Dewar used 10 minutes and Baird used 12. Neither showed that "20 minutes is optimal."

q: The higher the noise-reduction rating on the package, the more noise earplugs block.
head: False. Fit comes first.
why: If they aren't inserted properly, they won't block as much as the number says. Choose by whether they fit and don't hurt, ahead of a high number.

q: After sleeping with the overhead light on, the blood-sugar-lowering hormone worked less well the next morning.
head: True. One experiment found this.
why: Comparing a dark room with a 100-lux room, the lit night raised heart rate during sleep and insulin resistance the next morning. A small, short experiment.

q: With an eye mask, light most often leaks in beside the nose.
head: True. Check the fit around the nose.
why: Light most often leaks in beside the nose. Check whether there's extra fabric at the nose.

q: For the same amount of money, losses are thought to feel about twice as strong as gains.
head: True. It's called "loss aversion."
why: Kahneman and Tversky showed this tendency, and many later studies have estimated that losses are felt about twice as strongly as gains.

q: Looking back over long spans, people regret things they did more than things they didn't do.
head: False. What we didn't do lingers.
why: In the short term people regret actions, but over long spans, regrets about things they didn't do were more common and lasted longer.

q: People who reframed pre-performance anxiety as excitement did better on tasks like giving a speech.
head: True. One study found this.
why: A study by Brooks (2014). You may not be able to erase the body's reaction, but you can change what it means to you.

q: Get confident first, then act. That's the right order.
head: False. Often it's the other way round.
why: Act, fail a little, and learn you're still OK. Bandura (1977) also placed your own accomplishments as a key source of self-efficacy.

q: Impressions from seeing a stranger's face for 0.1 seconds closely matched unhurried judgments.
head: True. Even at 0.1 seconds.
why: In judging traits like attractiveness and trustworthiness, 0.1 seconds closely matched no-time-limit judgments. Trustworthiness matched especially well.

q: Viewing a face photo for longer changed people's impressions a lot.
head: False. Only their confidence changed.
why: Longer viewing didn't change the judgments much; what changed was people's confidence in them.

q: Even two nights of four-hour sleep made others less willing to spend time with someone.
head: True. No all-nighter needed.
why: After two nights of four-hour sleep, faces looked less attractive and healthy, and raters were less willing to spend time with them. Photo ratings, dozens of people.

q: Schopenhauer compared life to a pendulum swinging between pain and boredom.
head: True. A pendulum of pain and boredom.
why: Escape pain and boredom waits; escape boredom and desire and pain return. I also read in it: maybe the swinging itself is what living is.

q: Former Navy SEAL David Goggins did 4,030 pull-ups in 17 hours.
head: True. A Guinness World Record at the time.
why: In 2013, he did 4,030 pull-ups in 17 hours, setting what was then a Guinness World Record.

q: Goggins runs ultramarathons because he loves running.
head: False. He said, "I hate running."
why: Before the 2007 Badwater 135, he told a reporter "I hate running," then finished third. Not because he loves it, but because he decided to.

q: Goggins got through SEAL Hell Week on his first try.
head: False. Three times, including restarts.
why: He went through Hell Week, about 108 hours of cold and sleep deprivation, three times, including restarts after illness and injury.

q: If tongue coating bothers you, it's better to scrub with a tongue cleaner many times a day.
head: False. Once on waking, gently.
why: Once on waking is enough. More than that risks damaging the tissue. Not pressing too hard also matters.

q: Most bad breath is caused by stomach problems.
head: False. 80-90% starts in the mouth.
why: A systematic review gives oral factors as 80-90%. In 2,000 halitosis-clinic patients, 76% had a cause in the mouth; ENT or other outside causes were 4%.

q: Of 2,000 halitosis-clinic patients, 16% were diagnosed with pseudo-halitosis or halitophobia.
head: True. It's hard to judge your own breath.
why: Your own nose can't judge your breath accurately. On the other hand, some people don't notice until someone tells them.

q: Napoleon Hill's Think and Grow Rich says that if you wish hard enough, it comes true.
head: False. It's about turning wishes into action.
why: What it describes isn't magic but plain, practical steps: decide exactly what you want, set a deadline, make a plan and start moving.

q: One of Hill's steps is to write your goal down and read it aloud every day.
head: True. Along with a deadline and a plan.
why: His steps include deciding exactly what you want, setting a deadline, making a plan and starting to move, writing it down, and reading it aloud every day.

q: Declaring "From today, I'm this kind of person" is enough to change you.
head: False. You need small pieces of evidence.
why: Declaring it doesn't change you. Give your self-image small pieces of evidence, like reading ten pages or walking twenty minutes today.

q: In Japan, a recruitment agent's fee from the hiring company is about 5% of the new hire's annual salary.
head: False. About 30-35% of annual salary.
why: Generally about 30-35% (it varies by type of job). If someone earning 5 million yen joins, the company pays roughly 1.5 million yen.

q: Recruitment agents in Japan are free for job seekers because the hiring company pays.
head: True. The company pays when you join.
why: Most work on contingency: the company pays when a candidate joins. Japan's Employment Security Act in principle doesn't allow charging job seekers fees.

q: In an experiment where undecided people flipped a coin, those who chose change were happier about six months later.
head: True. Happier than those who stayed put.
why: Levitt's experiment. But participants were already undecided, so it's no basis for telling everyone to change jobs.

q: Job satisfaction that rises right after a job change stays high afterward.
head: False. It fell over the following year.
why: Satisfaction jumps after a job change, then declines over the following year. Researchers named this the "honeymoon-hangover effect."

q: As a rule, tell your current employer you're leaving only after you've accepted the offer.
head: True. The reverse puts you at a disadvantage.
why: Do it the other way round and you risk a gap in income or a weaker position in negotiations. As a rule, look for a job while still employed.

q: The best way to start a job search is by looking at job listings.
head: False. Start by sorting yourself out.
why: First decide why you want to leave and your priorities: two things you won't compromise on and two you can. Without that, every listing sways you.

q: If you like the work but the workplace doesn't suit you, you need to change careers.
head: False. Do the same work elsewhere.
why: Whether the problem is the work itself or the workplace and people makes a completely different answer for what to do.

q: A meta-analysis of 172 studies found that the better the person-workplace fit, the lower the intention to quit.
head: True. Satisfaction was higher too.
why: Better person-environment fit went with higher job satisfaction and organizational commitment, and lower intention to quit (Kristof-Brown et al., 2005).

q: A mini trampoline's weight limit is enough if it matches your body weight exactly.
head: False. Choose one with margin.
why: When you land, the mat takes more force than your body weight. Avoid numbers right at the edge; for family use, go by the heaviest person.

q: If noise is a concern in an apartment, a bungee mini trampoline suits better than a spring one.
head: True. Put a mat underneath too.
why: Bungees have no metal squeaking. Vibration still won't be zero, so use an anti-vibration or soundproofing mat and mind the time of day.

q: It's fine to tell your recruitment agent honestly that you're using other agents too.
head: True. It makes scheduling easier.
why: Agencies generally seem to expect it. Telling them makes scheduling easier than hiding it.

q: The more recruitment agents you sign up with, the better your chances.
head: False. Two or three is about right.
why: Too many means more meetings and messages, overlapping openings, and losing track of where you applied. With just one, you can't compare.

q: High-quality research has confirmed that music lessons make you smarter.
head: False. Transfer is close to zero.
why: A 2020 meta-analysis (54 studies, 6,984 people) found that, accounting for study quality, transfer to non-musical cognition or academics is close to zero.

q: Four-year-olds showed more spontaneous cooperation and helping after making music together.
head: True. More than without music.
why: In Kirschner and Tomasello's experiment, children who made music together helped and cooperated more than those in a control condition without music.

q: Pain thresholds rose the same way whether people sang and danced or only listened to music.
head: False. Not when only listening.
why: In Dunbar and colleagues' research, pain thresholds and positive affect rose after active music-making, but passive listening didn't show the same pattern.

q: Longer naps restore you more: 30 minutes leaves you sharper on waking than 10.
head: False. 30 minutes made it worse at first.
why: In an experiment with 24 sleep-restricted young adults, 10 minutes was most effective; 30 minutes worsened sleepiness and performance on waking (sleep inertia).

q: In one experiment, caffeine taken just before a nap led to less sleepiness after waking.
head: True. A small study of 10 students.
why: A Japanese experiment: caffeine before a 20-minute nap beat the nap alone or caffeine alone for sleepiness and performance. Just ten university students.

q: Nietzsche's "God is dead" simply means "there is no God."
head: False. It means more than that.
why: It asks why we keep living once we can no longer believe in the bigger something that gave us reasons to live.

q: Underarm odor is the smell of sweat itself.
head: False. Bacteria break it down into odor.
why: Research shows odor compounds arise when skin bacteria use enzymes to break down precursors that have little smell when first secreted.

q: Whether your earwax is wet or dry is linked to underarm odor.
head: True. The same gene is involved.
why: One difference in the ABCC11 gene decides earwax type and is involved in forming underarm odor compounds. But earwax alone can't tell you for certain.

q: In one experiment, smells too faint to consciously detect still changed how likable faces seemed.
head: True. Ratings changed.
why: People shown neutral faces while exposed to pleasant or unpleasant smells too faint to detect rated the faces' likability differently.

q: Japan's JAS standard has an "extra virgin" grade for olive oil.
head: False. There's no such category.
why: In Japan, JAS divides it only into "olive oil" and "refined olive oil." "Extra virgin" on Japanese shelves is the seller's label.

q: After 10 months stored under light, green glass bottles preserved olive oil better than cartons.
head: False. The cartons did better.
why: Multilayer paperboard cartons that block light curbed oxidation and kept antioxidant compounds better than green or UV-filtering glass bottles.

q: Compared with "other vegetable oils combined," olive oil showed no significant difference in cardiovascular risk.
head: True. No significant association.
why: Olive oil's strength lies less in beating other vegetable oils and more in being usable in place of butter, margarine and the like.

q: In a test heating ten cooking oils, EVOO was among those producing the most harmful compounds.
head: False. It was among the fewest.
why: Even at 180°C for a long time, EVOO was among those producing the fewest polar compounds. But it was a lab study heating oil alone, with limits.

q: In a US study, only about 5% of people were in the group consuming more than 7 g of olive oil a day.
head: True. Only about 5%.
why: 7 g is about half a tablespoon. It was still associated with lower risk, but the study was observational, so it can't show cause.

q: It's better to clean your tongue thoroughly, several times a day.
head: False. Once on waking is enough.
why: Japan's e-Health Net method: don't press too hard; once when you wake up is enough. Overdoing it can damage the tissue.

q: In a review of cleaning between teeth, interdental brushes did better than floss.
head: True. But the certainty is low.
why: A review of 35 studies found adding them may reduce gingivitis, with interdental brushes doing better. Certainty of evidence was low for both.

q: The extra muscle (fat-free mass) gained from protein supplements during strength training averaged about 0.3 kg.
head: True. The difference isn't big.
why: A meta-analysis of 49 trials found greater gains in strength and fat-free mass, but only about 0.3 kg in fat-free mass and about 2.5 kg in one-rep max.

q: Whey clearly beats soy for strength-training results.
head: False. No difference was seen.
why: A meta-analysis of nine studies found no difference in gains in strength or fat-free mass between soy and animal proteins such as whey.

q: Beyond about 1.6 g of protein per kg of body weight, more protein barely added muscle.
head: True. About 100 g a day at 60 kg.
why: A finding from the same meta-analysis. At 60 kg body weight, about 100 g a day is one guide to the upper limit.

q: In Japan, a regular employee needs the company's consent to quit.
head: False. The contract ends in two weeks.
why: With no fixed term, Article 627 of Japan's Civil Code lets you give notice, and the contract ends two weeks later even without the company's agreement.

q: In Japan, a private resignation-agency company can negotiate your paid leave for you.
head: False. It can only pass on the message.
why: Article 72 of Japan's Attorney Act bars non-lawyers from handling legal affairs for a fee. Negotiation needs a labor union or a lawyer.

q: The WHO classified burnout as a disease.
head: False. An "occupational phenomenon."
why: In 2019, the WHO placed burnout in ICD-11 not as a disease but as an "occupational phenomenon" resulting from chronic workplace stress.

q: Even in a busy job, people can get absorbed in their work if they have autonomy and support.
head: True. High demands aren't bad in themselves.
why: The problem is demands exceeding resources for a long time. If you want to quit, ask what's too much and what's missing.

q: If your annual pay dropped after a job change, your hourly pay must have dropped too.
head: False. It may have gone up.
why: It's not unusual for pay to drop only by the overtime you no longer do. Converted to an hourly rate, it may even have gone up.

q: In Japan, among people who changed jobs in 2024, 40.5% saw wages rise and 29.4% saw them fall.
head: True. Up 40.5%, down 29.4%.
why: From Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare 2024 Survey on Employment Trends. Put the other way, about 30% of job changers saw wages fall.

q: When a student asked Sartre for advice, he told him clearly which option to choose.
head: False. "You are free. Choose."
why: Avenge his brother, or stay with his mother? Sartre gave no answer: "You are free, so choose. That is to say, invent."

q: Sartre's "condemned to be free" means that if you hesitate and do nothing, you escape responsibility.
head: False. Doing nothing is also a choice.
why: We can't not choose; hesitating and doing nothing is also a choice. With no "essence" to use as an excuse, there's no escaping our choices.

q: The problem with believing "I can't do it" is that it directly causes failure.
head: False. It cuts the number of attempts.
why: A negative self-view cuts the number of attempts success requires. Over one, three, ten years, the gap in experience keeps growing.

q: To change your self-image, act small first and create "evidence."
head: True. No need to force the belief.
why: Want to be someone who exercises? Walk for 10 minutes. Bandura emphasized mastery experiences as one of the strongest sources of self-efficacy.

q: A human pheromone that attracts the opposite sex has already been confirmed.
head: False. None confirmed so far.
why: A strong argument from researchers is that no human pheromone has been established so far.

q: When men's scent was manipulated, women's ratings of them differed with videos but not photos.
head: True. The men's own behavior changed.
why: The scent changed the men's own confidence, and video ratings differed. Smell may change impressions through how the person carries themselves.

q: Memories triggered by smells tended to feel more emotional than those triggered by sights or sounds.
head: True. More emotional and evocative.
why: When someone's smell brings back the very scene where you met, this kind of background is probably at work.

q: College students who limited each social media app to 10 minutes a day had less loneliness and depression after 3 weeks.
head: True. Both went down.
why: An experiment with 143 people. But only college students, over a short three weeks, so we can't say the same change happens for everyone.

q: People who deactivated Facebook for four weeks knew more about the news.
head: False. Their news knowledge dropped a little.
why: Those who deactivated were slightly happier, but their knowledge of the news dropped a little. Social media isn't doing only bad things.

q: Epictetus counted your reputation among the things that are "up to us."
head: False. It's not up to us.
why: Up to us are judgment and what we pursue or avoid. The body, property, reputation, and position are not up to us.

q: Marcus Aurelius wrote the Meditations for the public to read.
head: False. It was a notebook for himself.
why: The Roman emperor wrote it in Greek, for himself, and it's thought he never meant to publish it.

q: Albert Ellis, who helped lay a root of cognitive behavioral therapy, often quoted Epictetus.
head: True. The founder of REBT.
why: Ellis frequently quoted the line that people are disturbed not by things but by their views of them. Ancient philosophy lives on in how we handle the mind.

q: A study of about 340,000 people found a clear "Blue Monday," with Monday uniquely bad.
head: False. Smaller than people assume.
why: There was a clear weekend effect, but Blue Monday wasn't as big as people assume. Maybe the heart of the pain is Sunday night.

q: Much of why weekends feel better came from choosing what you do and feeling connected.
head: True. Autonomy and relatedness.
why: In research by Ryan and colleagues, much of the weekend effect was explained by greater satisfaction of autonomy and relatedness.

q: In a beach study, people applied about a quarter of the sunscreen used to measure SPF.
head: True. About 0.5 mg/cm² on average.
why: SPF is measured at 2 mg per square centimeter. Apply less, and protection drops by more than the amount you cut.

q: People who applied sunscreen daily showed 24% less skin aging than those who used it at their discretion.
head: True. In a 4.5-year controlled trial.
why: A randomized controlled trial of 903 adults in Australia. What mattered wasn't a strong one now and then, but applying it every day.

q: A high SPF number tells you a sunscreen also blocks UVA, which reaches deeper into the skin.
head: False. Check the UVA rating for that.
why: SPF is mainly about UVB; PA (on Japanese labels) is mainly about UVA. If visible aging concerns you, check the UVA rating too.

q: In research, the time for a habit to become automatic varied widely, from 18 to 254 days.
head: True. About 66 days in their model.
why: From Lally and colleagues. Missing one opportunity didn't have much effect on forming the habit.

q: Miss even one day while building a habit, and habit formation is set back a lot.
head: False. It didn't have much effect.
why: In Lally and colleagues' study, missing once didn't have much effect. What you need is less perfection than the ability to come back.

q: Stepping on the scale every day to check the result is an example of a good system.
head: False. It's an example of a bad one.
why: A system that ends at checking the result is a bad one. A good system can explain how action leads to accumulation, then to results.

q: In a 14-week mini-trampoline study, older adults' ability to recover their balance improved by about 35%.
head: True. After losing balance forward.
why: Strength in the ankle-extending muscles rose about 10%. But these were older adults; it's not yet known if healthy working-age people would see the same.

q: Research has confirmed that trampolining clearly raises bone density.
head: False. No clear difference was found.
why: In a study of 40 women with osteopenia, strength and balance improved, but there was no clear group difference in spine or femoral neck bone density.

q: In a study of adults averaging 71, single-leg standing improved in the trampoline group.
head: True. Walking improved in both groups.
why: Six weeks of trampoline versus walking. But this alone doesn't show the trampoline is better.

q: Sleeping as much as you like on weekends prevented the drop in insulin sensitivity from sleep loss.
head: False. It didn't prevent it.
why: In an American experiment, even the weekend catch-up group didn't avoid the drop, and muscle and liver sensitivity got worse. A small, short experiment.

q: In a Swedish study, people sleeping 5 hours or less on weekdays but longer on weekends didn't have higher death risk.
head: True. In people under 65.
why: More than 43,000 adults followed for up to 13 years. But it was observational with self-reported sleep; other differences, like more slack in life, may matter.
